title: Basic sorts: selection, insertion, heap, merge
summary: The four classic comparison sorts — selection, insertion, heapsort and mergesort — with their exact intermediate states, best and worst runtimes, stability and memory use, plus inversions as the measure of how unsorted an array is. Exams show partially sorted arrays and ask which algorithm produced them, then probe runtime, stability and “which sort when”.

blocks.text: Sorts using only pairwise comparisons (compareTo / compare).
A pair of positions i < j with a[i] > a[j]. A sorted array has 0; a reversed array of N items has N(N − 1)/2 (28 for N = 8).
Items with equal keys keep their original relative order. Matters when sorting by one key after another.
Uses O(1) extra memory (O(log N) is often also accepted for recursion).
For i = 0, 1, …: find the smallest item in a[i..] and swap it into position i. After pass i, a[0..i] holds the i + 1 smallest items in final position.

blocks.title: Selection sort trace
blocks.prompt: Sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4], showing the array after each pass.
steps: i = 0: min 1 at index 3 → swap with 5: [1 2 8 5 9 3 7 4].

items: Always Θ(N²) comparisons (best = worst), at most N − 1 swaps.
In place. Not stable: a long-distance swap can jump an item over an equal one — sorting 3a, 1b, 3c, 2d, 1e by number gives 1b, 1e, 2d, 3c, 3a (3a and 3c reversed).

blocks.text: For i = 1, 2, …: take a[i] and swap it leftward while it is smaller than its left neighbour. After step i, a[0..i] is sorted (but not necessarily final).

blocks.title: Insertion sort trace
blocks.prompt: Sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4], showing the array after each i.
steps: i = 1: 2 moves left of 5: [2 5 8 1 9 3 7 4]. i = 2: 8 stays.
i = 3: 1 moves to the front: [1 2 5 8 9 3 7 4]. i = 4: 9 stays.
Total swaps: 1 + 0 + 3 + 0 + 3 + 2 + 4 = 13 — exactly the number of inversions.

blocks.name: Insertion sort and inversions
blocks.text: Each swap fixes exactly one inversion, so insertion sort does exactly K swaps for K inversions and runs in Θ(N + K). Best case (sorted) Θ(N); worst (reversed) Θ(N²). On almost-sorted input it is linear: an array of N items with one adjacent swap every 10 positions needed only N/10 swaps (100 for N = 1000, 200 for N = 2000) vs ≈ N²/4 for random input (248,481 and 1,004,912).

items: Stable (only adjacent unequal items swap) and in place.
Excellent for small arrays (Java uses it for subarrays below a small cutoff) and nearly sorted data.

blocks.text: Turn the array into a max-heap in place (bottom-up heapify, Θ(N)), then repeatedly swap the max (index 0) with the last unsorted position and sink the new root within the shrinking heap. With root at index 0, children of k are 2k + 1 and 2k + 2.

items: Θ(N log N) worst case; best case Θ(N log N) for distinct keys (Θ(N) if all keys are equal).
In place (O(1) extra), but not stable, and poor cache behaviour in practice.
Recognizable mid-trace: largest items in final position at the end, a max-heap in front.

blocks.text: Split in half, sort each half recursively, merge the two sorted halves with an auxiliary array. Merging N items costs Θ(N); T(N) = 2T(N/2) + N = Θ(N log N) in every case.

blocks.title: Mergesort trace (top-down)
blocks.prompt: Sort [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4]; show the array after each merge.
blocks.answer: Left half fully sorted before the right half starts (verified)

items: Θ(N log N) best and worst. Θ(N) extra memory for aux (not in place).
Stable as long as ties take from the left run (use <, not <=, in the comparison above).
Mid-trace signature: sorted runs of sizes 2, 4, … with the left part finished first (top-down).

blocks.text: * Θ(N) if all keys are equal. Java’s Arrays.sort on objects (TimSort) is a stable mergesort/insertion hybrid; on primitives it uses a (non-stable) dual-pivot quicksort, where stability is meaningless anyway.

blocks.title: Identify the sort from snapshots
blocks.prompt: Input [6, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 8, 4]. Each snapshot was produced mid-way by selection, insertion, heapsort (max-heap) or top-down mergesort. Identify: (a) [1 2 9 6 7 3 8 4] (b) [8 7 6 4 3 2 1 9] (c) [1 3 6 9 2 7 8 4] (d) [1 3 6 7 9 2 8 4] (e) [1 2 3 6 7 9 8 4].
steps: (a) Front holds the two smallest in final place, the rest is scrambled (6 has moved to where 1 was): selection after 2 passes.
(b) Largest item 9 at the end, a max-heap in front: heapsort after one removal.
(c) Runs [1 3 6 9] sorted and [2 7] sorted, rest untouched: mergesort after merge[4..5].
(d) Prefix [1 3 6 7 9] sorted but containing original items only (not the five smallest), suffix untouched: insertion after i = 4.
(e) Ambiguous! It is selection after 3 passes and also insertion after i = 5.
blocks.answer: (a) selection (b) heapsort (c) mergesort (d) insertion (e) selection or insertion (all verified)

blocks.text: Which sort when: nearly sorted or tiny → insertion; guaranteed N log N with O(1) memory → heapsort; stable N log N (sorting objects by several keys) → mergesort; minimal number of swaps/writes → selection.

hard.title: Count inversions in Θ(N log N)

prompt.text: Modify mergesort to return the number of inversions of the input in Θ(N log N). Explain the counting step and verify on [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 7, 4].

hard.answer: When an item is taken from the right run, add (mid − i + 1); 13 inversions

solution.text: Inversions split into: inside the left half, inside the right half (counted recursively), and cross pairs (left item > right item). When aux[j] (right) is output before aux[i], it is smaller than every remaining left item aux[i..mid]: that is mid − i + 1 cross inversions, each counted exactly once.
Returns 13 on the example, matching the brute-force count (verified). Same recurrence as mergesort: Θ(N log N).

hard.title: Identify the sorts

prompt.text: Input [6, 3, 9, 1, 7, 2, 8, 4]. For each snapshot list every algorithm among selection, insertion, heapsort (max-heap, root at 0, bottom-up heapify) and top-down mergesort that could have produced it at some point: (a) [1 3 6 9 7 2 8 4] (b) [9 7 8 4 3 2 6 1] (c) [1 2 3 4 7 9 8 6] (d) [3 6 1 9 7 2 8 4].

hard.answer: (a) insertion and mergesort (b) heapsort (c) selection (d) mergesort

solution.text: (a) Insertion after i = 3 gives [1 3 6 9 | 7 2 8 4]; mergesort after merge[0..3] gives the same array. Selection would have put 1 then 2 at the front; heapsort puts maxima at the end.
(b) That is exactly the heapified array (max at the root, no item yet moved to the end).
(c) The four smallest are in final place and the suffix 7 9 8 6 is a scrambled remainder: selection after 4 passes. Insertion’s prefix would contain the first five original items.
(d) [3 6] and [1 9] are sorted pairs, rest untouched: mergesort after merge[0..1] and merge[2..3]. All snapshots verified against instrumented sorts.

hard.title: Sort a k-sorted array

prompt.text: Every item of an N-element array is at most k positions from its sorted position. Sort it in Θ(N log k) time and Θ(k) extra space; compare with insertion sort. Why is Ω(N log k) comparisons necessary?

hard.answer: Sliding min-heap of size k + 1; insertion sort is Θ(Nk); lower bound from (k+1)!^(N/(k+1)) orderings

solution.text: Push the first k + 1 items into a min-heap. Then repeatedly removeMin into the next output slot and push the next input item. The true next item is always among the k + 1 candidates, so the output is sorted. Each heap operation is Θ(log k): Θ(N log k). On [2 1 4 3 6 5 8 7 10 9] with k = 1 this outputs 1 … 10 (verified).
Insertion sort: an item can only be inverted with items within distance 2k of it, so there are O(Nk) inversions and insertion sort costs Θ(N + Nk) = Θ(Nk) in the worst case.

Lower bound: split into N/(k + 1) blocks of k + 1 positions; each block can be any permutation independently, giving ((k + 1)!)^(N/(k+1)) inputs. log₂ of that is (N/(k+1))·Θ((k+1) log k) = Θ(N log k).

prompt.text: Records (key, tag): 3a, 1b, 3c, 2d, 1e. (a) Sort by key with selection sort; is the result stable? (b) With insertion sort? (c) You sort a list of students by name, then by section. Which sort must the second pass use so that, within each section, students appear alphabetically?

solution.text: (a) Pass 0 swaps 3a with 1b, sending 3a behind 3c eventually: final 1b 1e 2d 3c 3a (verified) — 3a and 3c reversed.
(b) Insertion only swaps adjacent unequal items: 1b 1e 2d 3a 3c (verified).
(c) The second (by section) sort must be stable so that ties in section keep the alphabetical order from the first pass — e.g. mergesort / Java’s object sort.

hard.title: Runtime puzzles

prompt.text: Give Θ for: (a) insertion sort on [N, 1, 2, …, N−1]; (b) insertion sort on [2, 3, …, N, 1]; (c) selection sort on a sorted array; (d) mergesort on a sorted array; (e) heapsort on an array of all-equal keys.

hard.answer: (a) Θ(N) (b) Θ(N) (c) Θ(N²) (d) Θ(N log N) (e) Θ(N)

solution.text: (a) The only inversions are N with each of the other N − 1 items: each new item swaps once past N, so N − 1 swaps in total: Θ(N).
(b) 1 forms N − 1 inversions; insertion moves it in the last step with N − 1 swaps: Θ(N).
(c) Selection always scans the rest: Θ(N²).
(d) Mergesort does the same splitting and merging: Θ(N log N) (without the “already ordered halves” shortcut).
(e) Heapify does no swaps, and every sink stops immediately: Θ(N).

hard.title: Mergesort with an insertion-sort cutoff

prompt.text: A hybrid mergesort stops recursing on subarrays of size ≤ k and sorts them with insertion sort. Give the worst-case runtime in terms of N and k, the k that keeps it Θ(N log N), and whether the hybrid is still stable.

hard.answer: Θ(Nk + N log(N/k)); any k = O(log N); yes, stable

solution.text: There are about N/k leaf subarrays, each sorted by insertion sort in Θ(k²) worst case: Θ(Nk) total.
Above the leaves the recursion has log₂(N/k) levels, each merging Θ(N) items: Θ(N log(N/k)).
Total Θ(Nk + N log(N/k)), which is Θ(N log N) whenever k = O(log N) (constant cutoffs like 7–32 are used in practice because insertion sort’s constant is tiny).
Both insertion sort and the left-preferring merge are stable, so the hybrid is stable (this is the idea behind TimSort).

keyFacts: Selection: Θ(N²) always, ≤ N swaps, in place, unstable.
Insertion: Θ(N + K) for K inversions (best Θ(N), worst Θ(N²)), in place, stable.
Heapsort: heapify Θ(N) + N sinks; Θ(N log N) worst, Θ(1) space, unstable.
Mergesort: Θ(N log N) always, Θ(N) aux space, stable (ties from the left).
Inversions: 0 sorted … N(N−1)/2 reversed; insertion sort swaps = inversions.
Snapshots: selection prefix = global smallest; insertion prefix = original items sorted; heapsort suffix = largest; mergesort = sorted runs.
Stable sorts preserve earlier orderings among ties (multi-key sorting).
